key_insight: Model-generated, domain-level skills can be systematically extracted from raw agent experience and meaningfully reused by downstream agents; the paper identifies which extraction and consumption design choices most affect utility and transferability.
problem_solved: Lack of a comprehensive, empirical understanding of how to turn raw agent trajectories into reusable, domain-level skills and how different extraction/consumption pipelines impact downstream performance and efficiency.
method: Assemble large-scale agent experience across multiple domains and tasks to serve as raw data for skill mining.

Apply and compare multiple model-driven extraction techniques (e.g., clustering of traces, prompt-based summarization, procedural distillation) and organize outputs into structured, domain-level skill artifacts.
Evaluate skill consumption by integrating mined skills into agents and measuring downstream gains on efficiency, generalization, and composability across domains.
impact: Provides practical guidance and empirical evidence for building scalable skill libraries that reduce manual engineering and speed domain adaptation for language agents; helps practitioners choose extraction and consumption strategies that maximize reuse and transfer.
visual_elements: Pipeline diagram: raw agent trajectories → skill extraction methods → skill library → agent consumption
Comparative bar chart: extraction methods vs. metrics (utility, generality, compactness, inference cost)
Example 'skill card' graphic showing inputs, steps, preconditions, postconditions, and prompts
Transfer heatmap: how skills mined in one domain improve performance in other domains (cross-domain transferability)
paper_title: From Raw Experience to Skill Consumption: A Systematic Study of Model-Generated Agent Skills
paper_authors: Zisu Huang, Jingwen Xu, Yifan Yang, Ziyang Gong, Qihao Yang
